https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An October 13, 2025 memo from Assistant Superintendent of Business Services Dan Trudel to Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky presenting two policy actions for Board approval. Policy 2002 (Learning and Achievement / graduation requirements) would be revised to require completion of "all legal requirements" and to add that the district will adopt administrative regulations implementing it. A new Policy 4003 (Employee Salary Schedules) would, per Michigan law, mandate normal salary schedules for non-bargaining-unit employees, delegating authority to the Superintendent to set them while requiring the Superintendent's own schedule to be approved by the Board yearly.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A memo transmitting two board policy changes for approval: a revision to Policy 2002 and a new Policy 4003.

Routing
- To: Dr. Richard Machesky, Superintendent
- From: Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services
- Date: October 13, 2025
- Subject: Policy Update and Administrative Regulation Update (2 policies)

Policy 2002 - Learning and Achievement (Graduation Requirements)
- Current: students must complete all coursework required by law, all district-required credits, coursework, and assessments, and other board requirements to graduate
- Recommended update: rewords to require completion of "all legal requirements, including coursework required by law," plus district credits, coursework, and assessments, and adds that "The School District will adopt Administrative Regulations implementing this policy."

Policy 4003 - Employee Salary Schedules (NEW)
- Per Michigan law, all employees must be paid pursuant to a normal salary schedule
- For employees not in a collective bargaining unit whose contract provides such schedules, the District will implement normal salary schedules setting base pay by job classification
- Job classifications for non-bargaining-unit employees are determined by the Superintendent
- The Superintendent is delegated authority to create and implement these schedules for all non-bargaining-unit employees, except the Superintendent, and must provide them to the Board before implementation
- The Superintendent's own normal salary schedule must be presented to the Board for approval yearly

Purpose
Seeks Board adoption of one revised and one new policy, addressing graduation requirements and statutory salary-schedule compliance.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum addressed to Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky from Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, dated October 13, 2025, transmitting a policy update and administrative regulation update for Board approval. Two policy actions are presented in total: a revision to an existing policy and the addition of a new policy.

The first item concerns Policy 2002 - Learning and Achievement, addressing graduation requirements. The current language states that in order to graduate and receive a high school diploma from the School District, a student must successfully complete all coursework required by law, all credits, coursework and assessments required by the School District, and all other requirements that may be established and published from time to time by the Board. The recommended update revises this to state that a student must successfully complete all legal requirements, including coursework required by law, all credits, coursework, and assessments required by the School District, and all other requirements that may be established and published from time to time by the Board, and it adds a new sentence: "The School District will adopt Administrative Regulations implementing this policy."

The second item is a recommended addition, Policy 4003, a new policy titled Employee Salary Schedules. It provides that, pursuant to Michigan law, all employees must be paid pursuant to a normal salary schedule. For those employees who are not part of a collective bargaining unit with a contract that provides normal salary schedules, normal salary schedules will be implemented by the District, setting out base pay for each job classification. Job classifications for non-bargaining-unit employees are to be determined by the Superintendent. The Superintendent is delegated the authority to create and implement normal salary schedules for all non-bargaining-unit employees - except for the Superintendent - but such salary schedules must be provided to the Board of Education prior to implementation. The normal salary schedule for the Superintendent must be presented to the Board of Education for approval on a yearly basis.

The memo frames these as policy updates for approval and references an accompanying administrative regulation update, aligning district policy with Michigan's statutory requirement that employees be compensated according to normal salary schedules. The two affected policies are identified by the headings Graduation Requirements (Policy 2002) and Employee Salary Schedules (Policy 4003).

Trudel summarizes a bell-time study conducted with School Bus Logistics (SBL) to evaluate later high school start times for Troy School District. It presents four routing scenarios plus in-house 3-tier and 4-tier options against the current 2024-25 baseline of 32 general-education buses on a 5-tier system, with each added route costing about $65,000 per year and each new bus about $170,000. The memo concludes the district cannot afford later start times now but could phase in routes over two years as a new middle school opens in Fall 2026.

What it is
A November 6, 2025 memo from Daniel C. Trudel, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, summarizing a bell-time study done in partnership with School Bus Logistics (SBL) on later high school start times.

Current baseline (2024-25)
- 32 general-education buses on a 5-tier system
- Each additional route costs roughly $65,000/year (route plus fuel); a new bus costs about $170,000

Scenarios analyzed (Gen-Ed routes only)
- Scenario A - Later HS start (8:00 AM), middle school earlier, elementary unchanged: +7 buses (39 total), $455,000 operating, $1,190,000 to purchase
- Scenario B - Swap elementary and middle school tiers: +11 buses (43 total), $715,000 operating, $1,870,000
- Scenario C - Combine middle and high school routes: +24 buses (56 total), $1,560,000 operating, $4,080,000
- Scenario D - Neighborhood node stops: +5-7 buses (37-39 total), $325,000-$455,000 operating, $850,000-$1,190,000
- In-house 4-tier option: +7 buses, $455,000, $1,190,000
- In-house 3-tier option: +14 buses, $910,000, $2,380,000

Next steps / purpose
The board must discuss implementation; the district can survey families but is not financially positioned to adopt later start times now. A new middle school opening Fall 2026 and another relocating create an opportunity to phase in routes over two years, including transportation for Boulan Park walkers to the old Smith Middle School and potential future service to TCCHS and the International Academy.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memo dated November 6, 2025 from Daniel C. Trudel, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, reporting the results of a bell-time study Troy School District conducted in partnership with School Bus Logistics (SBL). The study focused specifically on introducing later start times for high school students and assessed how different scheduling options would affect bus routes, staffing, and transportation efficiency. Four scenarios were analyzed using the district's current route data and software, while two further options (a 3-tier and a 4-tier system) were calculated in-house.

Current transportation overview: for 2024-25 the district operates 32 general-education buses under a 5-tier system. For costing, each additional route costs approximately $65,000 per year (route and fuel), and a new bus costs about $170,000 to purchase. Scenarios A through D factor in general-education routes only.

Scenario A - Later High School Start (8:00 AM): moves high school start from 7:20 to 8:00 a.m., adjusts middle school times earlier, and leaves elementary schools unchanged; requires 7 additional buses (39 total), an operational increase of $455,000, and bus purchases of $1,190,000. Scenario B - Swap Elementary and Middle School Tiers: switches the two time slots; requires 11 additional buses (43 total), $715,000 operating, and $1,870,000 in purchases. Scenario C - Combine Middle and High School Routes: places middle and high school students on the same buses; requires 24 additional buses (56 total), $1,560,000 operating, and $4,080,000 in purchases. Scenario D - Neighborhood Node Stops: uses fewer, centralized stops to shorten routes; requires approximately 37-39 buses (5-7 additional), $325,000-$455,000 operating, and $850,000-$1,190,000 in purchases.

Two in-house options were also modeled. A 5-tier to 4-tier conversion (general education only) would set high school at 7:45-2:38, middle school 8:17-3:05, early elementary 8:39-3:37, and late elementary 9:09-4:07, requiring 7 additional buses, $455,000 operating, and $1,190,000 in purchases. A 5-tier to 3-tier conversion would set high school 7:45-2:38, middle school 8:17-3:05, and elementary 8:50-3:48, requiring 14 additional buses, $910,000 operating, and $2,380,000 in purchases.

Next steps: the Board of Education will need further discussion on implementation, and the district can survey families and students to gauge interest. Trudel states the district is not in a financial position to implement later start times at present, but if the board desires the change there is opportunity to gradually build up route offerings over a two-year period. With a brand-new middle school opening in Fall 2026 and another middle school relocating buildings, additional drivers and routes will be needed to transport student walkers at Boulan Park to the old Smith Middle School. This creates an opportunity to expand routes to programs that currently lack transportation, potentially including in-district students who attend TCCHS and the International Academy.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL) presents its Bell Time Study report (Version 1.0, dated April 24, 2025) for Troy School District, prepared by Route Logistics Consultant Timothy Micheals for Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel. The report evaluates four scenarios, each adding a later start time for all high school students, using Versatrans RP routing software against a 2024-25 baseline. That baseline documents 32 vehicles required for general-education routing on the current 5-tier system, 153 daily labor hours, and 1,161 daily miles across the district's high schools, middle schools, and elementary schools.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The executive summary of a Bell Time Study prepared by School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL) for Troy School District, marked Version 1.0 and dated April 24, 2025. The transmittal letter from Timothy Micheals, Route Logistics Consultant (phone 331-575-2453, email tim.micheals@schoolbuslogistics.com), is addressed to Dan Trudel at Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and thanks Trudel and a staff member named Kathy for their collaboration.

Study overview: SBL was selected to conduct a bell-time study evaluating four distinct scenarios, and at the request of the school board each scenario incorporates a later start time for all high school students. Project objectives were to assess the current fleet schedule to establish a baseline, develop route packages aligned with bell-time options for each scenario, and ensure each scenario includes a later high school start. For each scenario SBL provides proposed bell times (AM arrivals and PM departures), an analysis of vehicle requirements, daily driver hours, and daily vehicle mileage.

Methodology: SBL used Versatrans RP routing software to develop route sets, focusing on General Education transportation. All data was housed on Troy School District's servers and accessed via a secure remote connection. Before analysis, data verification and cleanup addressed anchor sit times, stop sit times, and student load times. The baseline was documented using service windows at schools, total eligible riders (seat-capacity utilization), actual load counts provided by the district, and current route pairings.

Baseline data reflects the 2024-25 school year and includes vehicle requirements, travel time, and mileage. The current SY 2024-25 bell times are organized in five tiers. Tier 1: Athens High School and Troy High School, both 7:20 AM arrival and 2:08 PM dismissal, requiring 9 and 20 buses respectively. Tier 2: Larson Middle School and Boulan Middle School, both 7:52 AM and 2:40 PM, requiring 9 and 14 buses. Tier 3: Baker Middle School and Smith Middle School, both 8:17 AM and 3:05 PM, requiring 9 and 11 buses. Tier 4: Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, and Wattles elementary schools at 8:39 AM and 3:37 PM. Tier 5: Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard elementary schools at 9:09 AM and 4:07 PM.

Key baseline metrics: 32 vehicles are required for general-education routing under the current 5-tier system, with 153 daily labor hours and 1,161 daily miles. From this evaluation, four key tasks were identified, each summarized in the report. The document then begins Task 1 (Scenario A, High School Time Shift), which explores shifting the current high school arrival time from 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM; under this scenario Boulan Park and Larson middle schools would move to a 7:00 AM arrival while Baker and Smith would shift to 7:30 AM, with elementary arrival times unchanged and fleet pairings modified while maintaining the existing routing structure. The extracted text is truncated at this point in the report.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Director of Technology Saso Vasovski requests approval to spend $433,950.00 with Apple Inc. on iPads and cases to refresh 7th-grade devices for the 2025-26 year, upgrading from aging 7th-generation iPads (released 2019, 32GB, no longer supported by the latest iPadOS) to 11th-generation models. The memo, addressed to Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel and dated November 11, 2025, notes device generations have become inconsistent across grades due to out-of-band replacements, and that older still-supported devices will be pushed down to K-2 cart classrooms. The purchase would be funded by the Capital Projects fund.

What it is
A memo dated November 11, 2025 from Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, seeking approval for an Apple device purchase (Technology Services, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; 248.823.5060).

- Approval to purchase iPads and cases totaling $433,950.00 from Apple Inc.
- Refresh of 7th-grade iPads from 7th generation (the oldest in the district) to 11th generation

Why replace the 7th-generation iPads
- Device age: released in 2019, now over six years old, with slower performance and higher failure risk
- Limited storage: most have only 32GB, insufficient for standardized profiles and required apps, causing update failures
- OS compatibility: cannot run the latest iPadOS, blocking security updates and consistent device management

The original plan bought new iPads for 3rd and 8th graders each year, replacing a 3rd-grade device after five years when the student reached 8th grade. Out-of-band replacements for lost or broken devices made generations inconsistent across grades. Older devices still supported by Apple will be reassigned to Kindergarten through 2nd grade classrooms that use carts rather than take devices home. An attached multi-year iPad Refresh Plan details district-wide replacement.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum dated November 11, 2025 from Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, on the subject of an Apple purchase. The memo originates from Technology Services at 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.5060) and seeks approval to procure iPads and cases for a device refresh for the 2025-26 academic year.

The Teaching & Learning and Technology Services departments collaborated on a plan to upgrade the 7th-grade iPads from the 7th generation, the oldest generation in the district, to the newest 11th-generation iPad. The upgrade is intended to give students faster performance, longer battery life, better compatibility with the newest educational apps, more responsive multitasking, and upgraded storage, camera, and audio.

Three key reasons are cited for the recommendation. Device age: the current iPads were released in 2019 and are now over six years old, with aging hardware causing slower performance, reduced battery life, and increased failure risk. Limited storage: most units have only 32GB, which is insufficient for the district's standardized profiles and required applications and often results in update failures and app limitations. OS compatibility: the devices do not support the latest version of iPadOS, preventing access to critical security updates and new features and limiting the ability to enforce consistent device management policies.

The memo explains the district's original upgrade strategy was to purchase new iPads for 3rd-grade and 8th-grade students each year, the logic being to replace a brand-new 3rd-grade device after five years when the student entered 8th grade. Over time, device generations across grades became inconsistent because student devices that are broken or lost are replaced out of band, and an older-generation device is not always available for replacement; this creates situations where a student runs a newer-generation iPad than peers in the same grade. An attached iPad Refresh Plan document lays out a multi-year plan for device replacement across the district. Older devices that are still supported by Apple will be pushed down to Kindergarten through 2nd-grade classrooms, which use carts rather than taking devices home each day.

Vasovski requests approval for a purchase of $433,950.00 from Apple Inc. for Apple iPads and cases for the device refresh, and states the purchase will be paid for by the Capital Projects fund.

What it is
A resolution of the Troy School District Board of Education (County of Oakland, Michigan) authorizing the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), set for a regular meeting on November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m.

Authorization background
- November 8, 2022 election: voters approved bonds up to $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal) for remodeling/equipping buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds, a replacement middle school and classroom additions, instructional technology, site acquisition/improvement, and school buses
- First series: 2023 School Building and Site Bonds, dated March 7, 2023, $171,370,000 principal, issued with $18,629,212.85 net original issue premium counted against the $555,000,000
- Levies are unlimited as to rate or amount (Michigan Constitution 1963, Article IX)

What this resolution authorizes
- A second series of new-money bonds, aggregate principal not to exceed $193,000,000, for the Projects
- A current refunding of the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (dated December 28, 2016) maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032
- Combined new-money and refunding issue in a single series not to exceed $220,000,000, with a separate capital projects fund
- Fallback: if refunding becomes uneconomic, issue only up to $193,000,000

Sale and approvals
Negotiated sale; the Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent, Business Services (either acting as Authorized Officer) may accept an offer, negotiate and execute the bond purchase agreement. The district must obtain qualified status or prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury under Act 34.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, authorizing the issuance of 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation). The resolution is drafted for a regular Board meeting held in the School District on November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m. local time, with placeholders for present/absent members and the members offering and supporting the resolution.

Background recitals: at the General School Election held November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the '2022 Bond Proposal') for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom and other additions; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring, preparing, developing and improving sites; and purchasing school buses (the 'Projects'). Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for these bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount.

The district previously issued its 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 as the first series under the 2022 Bond Proposal; those bonds were issued with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which counts against the total $555,000,000 authorization. The Board now desires to authorize the second series under the 2022 Bond Proposal in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 to pay Project costs and a portion of issuance costs.

Under Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan 2001, as amended, the Board may refund funded indebtedness. The district previously issued its 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated December 28, 2016 (the 'Prior Bonds'), and the Board determines it is in the district's best interest to currently refund all or a portion of the Prior Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive (the 'Refunded Bonds'). Because the source of payment is the same, and to reduce issuance and administration costs, the Board finds it practical and economic to combine the new-money and refunding issues into a single series, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. If market interest rates rise so that refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board intends to retain the option of issuing only bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 for the Projects.

The district intends to sell the bonds by negotiated sale to preserve flexibility in timing and structure and to minimize issuance costs, and authorizes the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually as the 'Authorized Officer,' to accept an underwriter's offer to purchase, and to negotiate, approve and execute a bond purchase agreement and related documents. The district must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34 or receive prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury. The operative resolution designates the bonds '2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation),' issuable in one or more series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000 (or a lesser amount determined by the Authorized Officer upon sale), for financing a portion of the Project costs, refunding the Refunded Bonds, and paying issuance costs.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The external auditor's Report to the Board of Education for Troy School District (the School District) covers the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025, and is dated October 13, 2025. It is the auditor's formal governance communication, delivered alongside the audit report, and it bundles three sets of material identified by page range: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness, noting that audit preparation is performed on top of staff's normal daily activities.

Responsibility and standards: As stated in the engagement letter dated June 3, 2025, the auditor's responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management, with the Board's oversight, are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit is planned and performed to obtain reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement, and it does not relieve management or the Board of their responsibilities. Internal control was considered solely to design appropriate audit procedures, not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control.

Government Auditing Standards: The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. Under those standards the auditor must communicate certain matters, including compliance with provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; instances of error or fraud; illegal acts applicable to government agencies; and significant deficiencies in internal control. A separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses the auditor's consideration of internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance. The audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing previously communicated at the planning meeting on June 18, 2025.

Significant audit findings: Management is responsible for selecting and applying appropriate accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the School District adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the auditor's opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. The auditor noted no significant transactions recognized in the financial statements in a different period than when the transaction occurred. The most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the School District's share of the MPSERS net pension liability recorded under GASB Statement No. 68 and the net asset for the other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded under GASB Statement No. 75, both reported on the government-wide statements, because of their significance and the possibility that future events may differ significantly from the assumptions used.

The report exists to provide the Board with the information professional standards require the auditor to communicate about matters relevant to the Board's oversight of financial reporting. The report defines the relevant terms: a deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct, misstatements on a timely basis; a material weakness is a deficiency or combination of deficiencies such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis; and a significant deficiency is less severe than a material weakness yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance. The auditor states that its consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies. Given those limitations, during the audit the auditor did not identify any deficiencies in internal control that it considers to be material weaknesses, while cautioning that material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist that were not identified.

Report on Compliance and Other Matters: As part of obtaining reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement, the auditor performed tests of the District's compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements, noncompliance with which could have a direct and material effect on the financial statements. Providing an opinion on compliance with those provisions was not an objective of the audit, and no such opinion is expressed. The results of the tests disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters that are required to be reported under Government Auditing Standards.

Purpose: The report states that its purpose is solely to describe the scope of the auditor's testing of internal control and compliance and the results of that testing, and not to provide an opinion on the effectiveness of the District's internal control or on compliance. It is an integral part of an audit performed in accordance with Government Auditing Standards and is not suitable for any other purpose. The report was included in the materials for the Troy Board of Education Workshop held November 11, 2025.

Delivered as agenda item 8.A at the Troy Board of Education's regular meeting on November 18, 2025, this external auditor's board presentation covers Troy School District's financial results for the year ended June 30, 2025.

Audit highlights: the 2025 financial statement audit resulted in an Unmodified (clean) Opinion. For the 2025 federal program audit, the Compliance Supplement had not yet been issued, but the auditors anticipated issuing an Unmodified Opinion with no findings or questioned costs, having tested the Special Education Cluster. There were no findings on Bond and Sinking Fund Compliance or on Budgeting Act Compliance. The district held an ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2024.

Governmental funds (year ended June 30, 2025): the General Fund had revenue of $190,573,261 and expenditures of $193,633,993, an excess of expenditures over revenue of $3,060,732, reducing fund balance from $36,774,527 to $33,713,795. The 2023 Capital Projects Fund had revenue of $7,339,482 and expenditures of $57,874,218 (a $50,534,736 drawdown), reducing its balance from $177,897,535 to $127,362,799. Total Nonmajor Funds had revenue of $58,648,278 and expenditures of $56,904,267, increasing their balance from $14,821,514 to $16,565,525.

General Fund revenue by source: state source revenue $126,640,016 (66%), local revenue $46,912,097 (25%), interdistrict source revenue $13,039,291 (7%), and federal revenue $3,981,857 (2%). A foundation-allowance view breaks total revenue into the state portion of the foundation allowance $84,041,496 (44%), other state and local $58,993,621 (31%), property taxes $43,556,287 (23%), and federal $3,981,857 (2%).

General Fund expenditures by object: salaries and employee benefits $155,626,528 (80%), purchased services $28,321,325 (15%), supplies $7,239,540 (4%), and other expenses $2,446,600 (1%). By function, direct instruction was 64.48% of expenditures, above the Oakland County FY24 average of 58.34%, followed by indirect instruction 14.37%, operations and maintenance 7.76%, school administration 5.17%, pupil transportation 2.35%, general administration and business services 2.04%, central services 2.02%, athletics 1.39%, debt service 0.33%, and community services 0.09%.

Per-pupil trends: student population declined from 13,111 (2019-2020) to 12,074 (2025-2026), while the foundation allowance rose from $9,315 to $10,836 over the same period (labeled a 'Super Blend'). In a 2024-2025 comparison of foundation revenue per pupil among Oakland County districts, Troy's $10,394 ranked below Bloomfield Hills ($13,443), Birmingham ($13,363), Southfield ($12,410), Lamphere ($11,868), and Farmington ($11,484), and above West Bloomfield, Royal Oak, Novi, Walled Lake, Rochester, Waterford, and Huron Valley. Over the last ten fiscal years, General Fund fund balance ranged from about $21.5 million (15.35% of expenditures) in FY2016 to $33.7 million (17.41%) in FY2025, peaking at $36.8 million (19.21%) in FY2024; the statewide average fund balance as a percentage of expenditures for FY2024 was 24.7%.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Plante Moran's Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District, dated October 13, 2025, communicates the results of the firm's audit of the district's basic financial statements as of and for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025, together with other recommendations, observations, and informational items. The report is organized into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The auditors thank Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that preparing for the audit is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities.

Under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards, and as stated in the engagement letter dated June 3, 2025, the auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements, prepared by management with the Board's oversight, are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. GAAP; the audit provides reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement and does not relieve management of its responsibilities. As part of the audit the firm considered the district's internal control solely to design audit procedures, not to provide assurance on the effectiveness of that control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the auditors must communicate matters such as compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; certain instances of error or fraud; illegal acts applicable to government agencies; and significant deficiencies in internal control identified during the audit. A separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses the firm's consideration of internal control over financial reporting and its tests of compliance.

The audit was performed according to the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting held June 18, 2025. Among the significant audit findings, management is responsible for the selection and use of appropriate accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. Effective for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the district adopted Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the auditors' opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. The auditors noted no significant transactions recognized in the financial statements in a period different from when the transaction occurred. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This independent auditor's report from Plante Moran, addressed to the management and Board of Education of Troy School District, is the "Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance with Government Auditing Standards." It relates to the audit of the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining information of the district as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025, on which the firm issued its report dated October 13, 2025. The audit was conducted in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the Comptroller General of the United States.

On internal control over financial reporting, the report explains that in planning and performing the audit the firm considered the district's internal control to design audit procedures appropriate for expressing opinions on the financial statements, but not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control; accordingly, no such opinion is expressed. It defines a deficiency in internal control as existing when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct, misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is a deficiency, or combination, less severe than a material weakness yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance. The firm states its consideration of internal control was for a limited purpose and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies, and that during the audit it did not identify any deficiencies in internal control that it considers to be material weaknesses, while cautioning that unidentified material weaknesses or significant deficiencies may exist.

On compliance and other matters, the report states that as part of obtaining reasonable assurance about whether the district's financial statements are free from material misstatement, the firm performed tests of the district's compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements, noncompliance with which could have a direct and material effect on the financial statements. Providing an opinion on compliance with those provisions was not an objective of the audit, and none is expressed. The results of those tests disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters required to be reported under Government Auditing Standards. The report concludes that its purpose is solely to describe the scope of the firm's testing of internal control and compliance and the results of that testing, and not to provide an opinion on the effectiveness of the district's internal control or on compliance; it is an integral part of an audit performed in accordance with Government Auditing Standards and is not suitable for any other purpose. The report is dated October 13, 2025.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- The formal resolution of the Troy School District Board of Education (County of Oakland, State of Michigan) authorizing issuance of the "2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation)," offered at the regular meeting held November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m.

Background
- At the general school election on November 8, 2022, voters approved issuing bonds of up to $555,000,000 (the "2022 Bond Proposal") to remodel and equip facilities, erect a replacement middle school and classroom additions, install instructional technology, acquire and improve sites, and purchase school buses.
- The first series, the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds dated March 7, 2023, was issued at $171,370,000 with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85 (counted against the $555,000,000 authorization).

What it authorizes
- A second series of new-money bonds not to exceed $193,000,000 for the Projects.
- A current refunding of all or part of the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (dated December 28, 2016) maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032 (the "Refunded Bonds").
- Combining the new-money and refunding pieces into a single series not to exceed $220,000,000, while maintaining a separate capital projects fund; if refunding becomes uneconomic, the Board may instead issue only the up-to-$193,000,000 new-money bonds.

Key terms
- Unlimited-tax general obligation (Michigan Constitution of 1963, Article IX, Sections 6 and 16); refunding authorized under Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001.
- Negotiated sale; the Superintendent and Assistant Superintendent, Business Services (either acting individually, the "Authorized Officer") may accept the underwriter's offer and execute the bond purchase agreement.
- Requires qualified status or prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Offered at the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education (County of Oakland, State of Michigan) held November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m. local time, this is the full preamble and resolution "Authorizing 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation)," with blanks for members present and absent and for the members offering and supporting it.

The recitals establish the authorization history. At the General School Election held November 8, 2022, the district's qualified electors approved issuing bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the "2022 Bond Proposal") for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing buildings; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring, preparing, developing and improving sites, plus the purchase of school buses (the "Projects"). Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The district previously issued its 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 as the first series under the 2022 Bond Proposal; because of prevailing market conditions, those bonds carried a net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which is counted against the $555,000,000 authorization.

The Board now desires to authorize the second series under the 2022 Bond Proposal in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 to pay Project costs and a portion of issuance costs. Under Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended ("Act 34"), the Board may refund all or part of the district's funded indebtedness; the district previously issued its 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated December 28, 2016 (the "Prior Bonds"), and the Board determines it is in the district's best interest to currently refund all or a portion of the Prior Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive (the "Refunded Bonds"). Because the source of payment is the same, and to reduce issuance and administration costs, the Board finds it practical and economical to combine the new-money and refunding issues into a single series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. If market interest rates rise so that refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board intends to retain the option of authorizing only the up-to-$193,000,000 new-money bonds for the Projects. The district desires a negotiated sale to preserve maximum flexibility in timing and structure and to minimize issuance costs, and deems it advisable to authorize the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services — either one acting individually (the "Authorized Officer") — to accept an underwriter's offer to purchase the bonds, negotiate, approve and execute a bond purchase agreement, and approve various other terms and documents in connection with the sale and delivery. The district must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34 or receive prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

The resolving clauses provide that the bonds, designated "2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation)," be issued in one or more series (with changes to the name, designation, or suffix as appropriate for each series based on the type of bonds issued) in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, or such lesser amount as the Authorized Officer determines upon sale, for the purpose of financing a portion of the Projects, refunding the Refunded Bonds, and paying the costs of issuance. The extracted text ends as it begins describing the portion of the bonds issued to finance the Projects.

This memorandum, dated November 11, 2025, is from Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, regarding an Apple purchase. Technology Services is located at 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.5060). Vasovski seeks approval to procure iPads and cases for a device refresh for the 2025-26 academic year.

The core proposal, developed jointly by the Teaching & Learning and Technology Services departments, is to upgrade the 7th-grade iPads — the oldest generation in the district, currently 7th-generation devices — to the newest 11th-generation iPad. The memo argues the upgrade gives students faster performance, longer battery life, better compatibility with the newest educational apps and tools, more responsive multitasking, and upgraded storage, camera, and audio. Three specific justifications are given: (1) Device age — the 7th-generation units were released in 2019 and are now over six years old, with aging hardware leading to slower performance, reduced battery life, and increased risk of failure; (2) Limited storage — most units have only 32GB, which is insufficient for the district's standardized profiles and required applications, often resulting in update failures and app limitations; and (3) OS compatibility — the devices do not support the latest version of iPadOS, preventing access to critical security updates and new features and limiting the ability to enforce consistent device-management policies.

The memo describes the district's device-refresh strategy. The original plan was to purchase new iPads for 3rd-grade and 8th-grade students each year, so that a brand-new 3rd-grade device would be replaced after five years upon the student entering 8th grade. Over time, the generation of devices across grades became inconsistent because student devices that are broken or lost must be replaced "out of band," and an older-generation device is not always available for replacement — creating situations where a specific student runs a newer-generation iPad than peers in the same grade. An attached "iPad Refresh Plan" document lays out a multi-year plan of device replacement across the district. Older devices still supported by Apple will be pushed down to Kindergarten-through-2nd-grade classrooms, which utilize a cart rather than sending devices home each day.

The memo requests approval for a purchase of $433,950.00 from Apple Inc. for Apple iPads and cases for this device refresh, and states the purchase will be paid for by the Capital Projects fund.

A recommendation memorandum supporting Board Item 8.G, from Shari Pawlus, Supervisor of ELD, K-12, to the Troy School District Board of Education. Dated October 2, 2025. Subject: approval of the Language Power curriculum for elementary schools.

Background / pilot
During 2024-25, elementary ELD specialists piloted Language Power across multiple sites, with focused study sessions, job-embedded professional development in real classrooms, and coaching from the program's teacher-developer (a former ELD specialist). Afterward, 85% of specialists agreed Language Power is the most effective and comprehensive resource for the district's multilingual learners.

A research-based, standards-aligned curriculum for multilingual learners that builds academic vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing. It includes teacher kits with structured lesson plans, student anthologies of leveled texts, consumable student practice workbooks, and digital access (reducing annual repurchasing). The vendor also includes professional development this year: an "unpacking" launch session plus ongoing job-embedded coaching/PD.

- Teacher Kits (General Funds): $22,000
- Supplemental Materials (Title III): $70,000 - anthologies, consumable workbooks, and digital licenses

Recommendation
Pawlus recommends the Board approve the purchase of Language Power for elementary ELD programming to provide multilingual learners equitable access to high-quality instruction.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
What it is
A memorandum recommending a curriculum purchase, supporting Board Item 8.G. Addressed to the Troy School District Board of Education from Shari Pawlus, Supervisor of ELD (English Language Development), K-12, and dated October 2, 2025. Subject: Approval of Language Power Curriculum for Elementary Schools.

Background and pilot
During the 2024-25 school year, the district's elementary ELD specialists piloted Language Power across multiple sites. As part of the pilot, specialists engaged in a comprehensive professional learning plan: they explored the materials in focused sessions, participated in job-embedded professional development using the curriculum in real classrooms, and received coaching from the program's teacher-developer, a former ELD specialist. Following the pilot, 85% of specialists agreed that Language Power is the most effective and comprehensive resource to meet the district's multilingual learners' language development needs.

Program description
Language Power is described as a research-based, standards-aligned curriculum designed specifically for multilingual learners, building academic vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing skills through interactive lessons and scaffolded support. The program includes: teacher kits with structured lesson plans; student anthologies providing leveled, engaging texts; consumable student practice workbooks; and digital access to resources that reduces the need for annual repurchasing. The memo emphasizes that the combination of consumables and digital resources gives students both hands-on materials and technology-supported access for flexible instruction.

Professional learning
In conjunction with the quoted pricing, the vendor agreed to provide additional professional development during the school year, including an "unpacking" session to launch the materials plus ongoing job-embedded coaching/PD to support high-fidelity classroom implementation. This support is included in the quoted price.

Funding plan
To implement Language Power districtwide at the elementary level, the memo proposes:
1. Teacher Kits, funded from General Funds - cost $22,000 - providing the core teacher materials necessary to deliver instruction.
2. Supplemental Materials, funded from Title III - cost $70,000 - including anthologies, consumable student workbooks, and digital licenses. With digital access, the district avoids purchasing replacement materials year after year, creating a sustainable model for ongoing use.

Recommendation
Based on the successful pilot and strong support from specialists, Pawlus recommends that the Board approve the purchase of Language Power for elementary ELD programming, stating it will provide multilingual learners with equitable access to high-quality instruction and resources that support their academic growth and language development.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A November 2025 Board of Education data presentation, 'Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action,' summarizing Troy School District results on the 2024-2025 Michigan state assessments. Troy outperformed Oakland County and statewide averages across M-STEP (grades 3-7), PSAT 8, and SAT 11 in both ELA and math; district grades 3-7 ELA proficiency reached 67.9% and math 77.9%. The presentation also examines persistent performance/opportunity gaps for students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners, and describes the district's Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) response.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A district data review presented to the TSD Board of Education in November 2025, titled 'Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action.' It covers state-assessment proficiency, trends over time, district/county comparisons, and gaps between student groups, noting that state tests are summative snapshots, not diagnostic tools.

M-STEP grades 3-7 (2025)
- ELA proficiency by grade: 67.9 / 66.3 / 67.9 / 64.5 / 66.1
- Math proficiency by grade: 77.9 / 65.9 / 65.5 / 65.8 / 68.4

Trends and comparisons
- 3-7 ELA proficiency: TSD 67.9% (SY25) vs Oakland 49.8%, statewide 38.9%
- 3-7 Math proficiency: TSD 77.9% (SY25) vs Oakland 55.4%, statewide 42.7%
- PSAT 8: ELA 83.5%, Math 64.3% (2025); SAT 11: ELA 79.3%, Math 60.7% (2025)
- M-STEP Science (Gr 5/8/11): 61.1 / 65.3 / 50.2; Social Studies: 51.0 / 68.1 / 56.9

Gap analysis
Special-education performance gaps are quantified by grade (roughly 45-53 in ELA and 39-54 in math across grades 3-11). Gaps are framed as an 'Opportunity Gap' for students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners.

Purpose
Identify areas of focus and celebration and commit to MTSS: coherent systems, Professional Learning Communities, Tier 1 instruction, universal supports, progress monitoring, content-strong interventionists, and a district handbook.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Troy School District Board of Education presentation from November 2025 titled 'Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action,' reporting student performance on 2024-2025 Michigan summative state assessments (M-STEP, PSAT 8, SAT 11) with district-by-district and over-time comparisons and an analysis of gaps between student groups. The deck stresses that state assessments are a snapshot within a balanced assessment system and are not designed to be diagnostic or to drive day-to-day teaching.

M-STEP grades 3-7, 2025 percent advanced/proficient by grade: ELA 67.9, 66.3, 67.9, 64.5, 66.1 (2024: 63.2, 66.8, 69.0, 64.4, 64.8); Math 77.9, 65.9, 65.5, 65.8, 68.4 (2024: 72.4, 68.9, 64.1, 66.3, 66.0).

Proficiency over time (grades 3-7): ELA TSD fell from 74.0% (SY19) through 69.1%, 65.9%, 63.2% to 67.9% (SY25), well above Oakland (49.8%) and statewide (38.9%). Math TSD moved 75.0% to 77.9% (SY25) vs Oakland 55.4% and statewide 42.7%. In county comparisons Troy led with roughly 71% ELA and 71% math proficiency.

PSAT 8 / SAT 11: ELA grade 8 was 84.2% (2024) and 83.5% (2025); grade 11 was 77.3% (2024) and 79.3% (2025). Math grade 8 held at 64.3% and grade 11 was 60.7% (2025). Grade-8 ELA over time: TSD 83.5% (SY25) vs Oakland 74.5%, state 65.3%; grade-8 Math: TSD 64.3% vs Oakland 42.4%, state 30.4%. Grade-11 ELA: TSD 79.3% vs Oakland 64.1%, state 55.4%; grade-11 Math: TSD 60.7% vs Oakland 37.4%, state 27.5%. SAT county comparison shows Troy grade-11 EBRW at 79.3% and Math near the top of Oakland districts.

M-STEP Science (grades 5, 8, 11), 2025: 61.1%, 65.3%, 50.2% (2024: 62.6%, 64.4%, 46.3%). M-STEP Social Studies (grades 5, 8, 11), 2025: 51.0%, 68.1%, 56.9%, up from 34.9%, 47.5%, 46.6% in 2024.

The Gap Analysis section addresses ELA and math and notes that districts have historically struggled to raise performance of Students with Disabilities, Economically Disadvantaged Students, and English Learners to countywide/statewide rates, a phenomenon described as the Performance Gap or Opportunity Gap. Special-education performance gaps for 2025 are charted by grade (3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11): ELA values 45.4, 49.4, 47.7, 49.8, 52.3, 53.1 and Math values 39.1, 40.9, 46.7, 49.3, 54.1, 51.7, with a further subgroup gap chart (values 29.5, 24.2, 30.8, 27.2, 20.8, 25.7 and 22.6, 28.4, 32, 35.2, 41.4, 40.1).

Implications and actions center on a Multi-Tiered System of Support: district commitment to building coherence, focus on systems that support all students, Professional Learning Communities in process at all schools, universal supports, review and progress monitoring of any student on a plan, development of a district handbook, interventions taught by content-strong teachers, and a focus on Tier 1 instruction. The stated purpose is to highlight both celebrations and areas of focus.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of a Troy Board of Education regular meeting held Tuesday, October 14, 2025 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Vice President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mrs. Anne, board members Alic, Haupt, Melton, Potts, and Zendler were present; President Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Pagel, Zawislak, Cottone, Vasovski, and Trudel, with approximately 12 audience members.

Recognitions opened the meeting with a TSD Mission Moment. The Board presented the Apple Distinguished School Award to Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, an honor recognizing schools as centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence with a clear vision for learning with technology; fewer than a thousand schools worldwide hold the distinction. Additional recognitions included Learning Disabilities Awareness Month, 2025 Principals Appreciation Month, and the 2026 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists.

The Board considered Additions and Deletions, Public Communication on agenda items, and a General Consent Agenda. Under Personnel, the agenda included an Administrative Appointment for Director of Technology. Under Business, items included an Administration Building furniture purchase, cafeteria tables for Barnard Elementary, and technology upgrades and access control. The meeting also included reports from High School Student Representatives and Board Comments.

A formal resolution designated October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month. It was moved by Dr. Melton and supported by Mr. Haupt. The resolution's WHEREAS clauses state that learning disabilities refer to differences in how brains work that may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that they range in severity and may impact oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity though individuals may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths; and that appropriate supports, specialized assessments, and interventions across home, school, community, and workplace can enhance quality of life. The resolution resolves that the Troy School District Board of Education joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart; the resolution was adopted. Minutes were prepared under the notation EA/jh.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A staff recommendation presentation titled 'Recommendations for Schools of Choice, 2026-2027 School Year,' prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent Secondary Instruction, and Kristine Griffor, Assistant Superintendent Elementary Instruction, and dated Tuesday, December 9, 2025. The deck explains that Schools of Choice provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities, that participation is optional for districts, and that the degree and extent of participation - including application/enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment - are determined locally.

Enrollment projections (submitted by Plante Moran Cresa) track kindergarten and first grade. For 2025-2026 the most-likely kindergarten figure is 778 (707 Kdg / 71 PreK) with first grade 786; for 2026-2027 the projection is 766 kindergarten (686 Kdg / 80 PreK) and 739 first grade. Non-Schools-of-Choice enrollment for 2025-2026 totals 11,165 students across grades K-12.

Current Schools of Choice data for 2025-2026: 173 elementary SOC students against 4,708 non-SOC students, or 3.54% SOC district-wide. By building, the highest SOC shares are Hill Elementary 10.57% (39 SOC), Wass 6.35% (25), Wattles 5.54% (22), Hamilton 4.70% (22), Costello 4.04% (16), Troy Union 3.90% (15), Martell 3.26% (11), Leonard 3.09% (13), Barnard 1.73% (7), Morse 0.51% (2) and Bemis 0.24% (1); Schroeder Elementary has 0 SOC students. By grade, SOC counts are kindergarten 37, first 33, second 14, third 22, fourth 32 and fifth 35. Demographically, SOC students are 55.49% White, 16.18% Asian, 12.72% Black, 9.83% multi-ethnic and 5.20% Hispanic; 54.34% qualify for Free/Reduced Lunch (vs. 28.91% of non-SOC), 19.65% receive Special Education (vs. 13.87%), and 10.98% are English Learners (vs. 24.92%).

A sibling-preference survey was emailed to current Schools of Choice families to identify siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade, and grades 6-8 (Baker Middle School) in 2026-2027. Results: kindergarten - 8 for Section 105 (in-county) and 4 for Section 105c (out-of-county); first grade - 0 for Section 105 and 1 for Section 105c; middle school grades 6-8 combined - 2 for Section 105 and 1 for Section 105c.

The staff recommendation proposes Section 105 (in-county) slots totaling 100 - comprising 75 for kindergarten and 25 for first grade - plus the 10 known Section 105 siblings, and Section 105c (out-of-county) slots comprising 6 known siblings. Factors cited for the recommendation include current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; the numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of age-eligible Schools of Choice siblings; and available elementary classrooms.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The 2026 Member District Ballot issued by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) for its member boards, including the Troy School District Board of Education, to record their vote on OCSBA's proposed resolutions. The ballot explains OCSBA's process: annually the Government Relations Committee (GRC) establishes legislative priorities for the current session; the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee then reviews those priorities and drafts new resolutions and/or amendments, referencing aligned MASB and/or NSBA resolutions where applicable. After Board of Directors review, proposed resolutions are presented to member districts. Member districts vote only on proposed new or amended resolutions - continuing resolutions are not subject to re-vote - and resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association. Each member district receives one vote.

On the voting period, the ballot states that the proposed resolutions, legislative priorities, and ballot were transmitted to every member and all member district executive assistants on November 18, 2025, that the voting period remains open for at least forty (40) calendar days, and that completed ballots must be received no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, January 9, 2026. Ballots must be completed, signed, and returned to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org before the deadline or the district's vote cannot be counted, per OCSBA bylaws Article III, Section 2, under which member votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees.

The ballot poses a single question - 'Does the Board of Education approve the proposed new and/or amended resolutions as presented?' - with blanks for the district name and meeting date and two options: YES (the Board approves all proposed new resolutions as presented) or NO (the Board does not). A certification section attests that the record is a true and correct record of the Board's vote, to be signed by the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board of Education and Superintendent, with printed name and signature. Questions are directed to Stefanie Crane (scrane@clarkston.k12.mi.us). The document is a voting form; it does not itself record how Troy voted.

Proposed Resolution #2 supports full funding of Early On Michigan, the state's Part C early-intervention program for infants and toddlers birth to age three; it cites an estimated $230M annual cost, a recommended state appropriation of at least $138M, versus $48M provided under Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) proposed resolutions document for January 2026, listing two proposed new resolutions and previously adopted continuing resolutions. Per OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, resolutions approved by at least 19 member school districts become the association's official position.

Proposed new resolution #1 - Non-partisan school board elections
OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections, in response to HB 4588 moving through the Michigan House. It argues partisan elections would decrease willing candidates, increase campaign costs (a primary plus the November election), align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs, and exclude federal employees legally barred from partisan races.

Proposed new resolution #2 - Early On Michigan funding
OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, the state's Part C (IDEA) early-intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at-risk conditions. Estimated annual cost is $230M; the state should appropriate at least $138M (60%); Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides $48M.

Continuing resolutions (previously adopted)
- Accountability and Transparency (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025)
- Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025)
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) proposed resolutions packet dated for January 2026, combining two proposed new resolutions with a list of continuing (previously adopted) resolutions. It opens by citing OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 (Resolution Adoption): resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

Proposed new resolution #1 states that OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The rationale ties it to House Bill 4588, then moving through the Michigan House (a link to the bill is provided). It argues that partisan school board elections would decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, because members would have to win two elections (a primary as well as the November election); align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

Proposed new resolution #2 states that OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale explains that Michigan's Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires services for eligible children from birth through age 25; that under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), Part B covers ages 3 through 21 and Part C covers eligible infants and toddlers from birth through age 2 (called Early On in Michigan); and that services for ages 22 through 25 fall under MMSE. Early On is coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education under IDEA Part C, with local funding flowing through Intermediate School Districts (ISDs) and interagency coordinating councils. The resolution notes the long-standing federal promise to fund 40% of special education costs and states that state funding for Early On is lacking: the estimated annual cost is $230M for high-quality early intervention services, the state should appropriate at least $138M (60% of the estimated cost), while Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides only $48M.

The document then lists continuing resolutions previously adopted by members, with adoption and amendment dates. 'Accountability and Transparency' (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025) holds every school receiving public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and colleges and universities, referencing MASB Resolution A 6.65. 'Broadband Access and Devices' (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025) supports including broadband in federal or state infrastructure plans, additional funding to expand affordable and reliable broadband access, and programs to purchase internet-capable devices and software. The extracted text is truncated within the continuing-resolutions section.

It notes the current textbooks - Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French - are outdated, lack current cultural content, and offer no AP test prep. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Instructional presentation to the December 9, 2025 Board of Education Workshop on the AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption for the Troy School District World Language program.

Context
- The World Language sequence runs Levels 1-5, with AP at the top; AP exams are written at intermediate-high/advanced levels.
- AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate-level college course covering family/communities, identities, beauty/aesthetics, science/technology, contemporary life, and global challenges.
- World Languages run on a 7-year adoption cycle.

Current state
- Resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture.
- Abriendo Paso (2014, AP Spanish): outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice, no AP test prep.
- T'es Branche (2014, AP French): a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources.
- Teachers currently assemble materials from many sources, some at their own cost.

Selection process
Guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. Timeline: 2024-25 exploration; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff/visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning/check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

Vendors and recommendation
- Wayside (French/Spanish): relatable, authentic content but does not match AP rigor; textbook only, no assessment practice.
- Klett: no AP French resource; Spanish has authentic resources and AP practice but less rigor, fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology.
- Vista Higher Learning (French/Spanish, recommended): matches AP-exam rigor, culturally relevant, large resource bank; authors are College Board trainers; about 80% AP World Languages market share; will provide a crosswalk and free updated resources for the revised 2026-27 AP exam.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on December 9, 2025, this slide deck makes the case for adopting new AP Spanish and AP French instructional resources within the district's World Language program.

Context and rationale: The World Language sequence runs from Level 1 through Level 5 (AP), and the AP exams are written at the intermediate-high/advanced levels. The presentation cites the TSD World Languages Vision, which holds that language learners can communicate in an expanding global community, experience another culture's heritage, become resilient risk-takers, improve memory and problem-solving, strengthen college applications and professional marketability, and open opportunities for world travel. AP World Language and Culture is described as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course in which students apply interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational modes of communication across themes of family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the district's 2017-adopted resources do not represent current culture.

Current state: World Languages operate on a 7-year adoption cycle, and with the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers want a common resource to build cohesion across programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish - criticized for outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice, and no AP test prep - and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is actually a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. In current reality, teachers pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own cost.

Selection process: The work was guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. The AP resources timeline included exploration during the 2024-25 school year, leadership planning on 8/11, department kickoff and visioning on 8/20, rubric creation and vendor presentations on 10/2 and 10/7, pilot planning on 10/20, PLC planning and check-ins on 11/11 and 11/18, and pilot feedback and synthesis on 12/2.

Vendors considered: Wayside (French and Spanish) offered relatable, authentic content but did not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and was a textbook without assessment practice. Klett had no AP French resource; its Spanish resource had many authentic materials and AP practice but did not match AP rigor, offered fewer resources than Vista, and had less user-friendly technology. Vista Higher Learning (French and Spanish) matched the rigor of the AP exam, provided meaningful, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank (though some may need scaffolding early in the year); its authors are also College Board trainers, and it holds about 80% of the AP World Languages market share. For the updated 2026-27 AP exam, Vista agreed to provide an updated crosswalk and, when it updates its textbooks, to supply updated electronic and physical resources free of cost, with the district banking professional-learning credit in August to support the change. The deck closes with features of the recommended texts, including culturally relevant AP French resources and an AP Spanish cultural-comparison example.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on December 9, 2025, this athletics update was delivered by Matt Jansen, TSD Director of Athletics, alongside athletic coordinators Todd Heugh (Athens) and Karen Baird (Troy High). It covers fall sports, sports offered, participation rates, budget, the student-athlete handbook, communications, certifications, and community partnerships.

Fall sports highlights: Troy High boys varsity tennis were State Champions; Athens boys varsity soccer were State Semifinalists; the Troy United boys varsity water polo team members were all Academic All-State; Todd Heugh was inducted into the HSSHOF; the Athens and Troy varsity boys soccer teams were Division 1 Regional Finalists; and girls flag football was piloted as a club. The district also noted it is about one year from completing all sports bond projects.

Bond athletic facilities: At Troy High, projects include a new stadium and auxiliary turf fields (2024), tennis courts (2025), track (2025), scoreboards (2025-26), varsity and JV baseball and softball fields (2026), bathrooms and athletic storage (2026), and a new gymnasium floor and bleachers (2026). At Athens, projects include a new gymnasium floor and bleachers (2024), a new stadium, concessions, and auxiliary turf fields (2024-25), baseball and softball fields (2025), bathrooms and storage (2025), tennis courts (2025), scoreboards (2025), and a new track (2026).

Program scope: TSD sponsors 31 varsity sports (2 of them club) plus 10 non-MHSAA club sports, fielding more than 100 teams with approximately 1,700 unique student-athletes annually and about 250 MHSAA coaches. MHSAA-sponsored sports span boys, girls, and coed offerings; non-MHSAA club sports include boys water polo, power lifting, rugby, sailing, and volleyball, and girls flag football, hockey, power lifting, synchronized swim (a varsity sport), dance, figure skating, sailing, and water polo.

Participation: In 2024-25, 40% of high school students participated (1,697 of 4,280) and 48% of 7th and 8th graders participated (950 of 1,990), for a combined 2,647 student-athletes - up 101 (4%) from 2,546 in 2023-24. Prior years were 2,456 (2022-23), 2,408 (2021-22), and 1,769 (2020-21, Covid).

Budget and revenue: The 2024-25 athletics budget totaled $2,689,272 - Coaches $1,303,265 (48%), Officials $166,845, Athletic Training $132,379, Game Management Staff $75,044, and Expenses $1,011,739 - plus Transportation of $85,639. Athletics revenue totaled $678,178 (Pay-to-Participate $407,025; Gate Receipts $187,521; Event Passes $83,632), an increase of $112,411 over 2023-24, offsetting the budget to a net of $2,011,094. The presentation frames this as a return on investment of 1.4% of the TSD budget benefiting 2,647 student-athletes in grades 7-12. Pay-to-participate fees are $200 per sport at the high schools and $100 at the middle schools, with the third sport free and a $600 family maximum; gate fees are $7.00 (senior rate $5.00, Troy resident seniors free), with adult passes $80, two-adult passes $120, and student passes $60.

Other initiatives: The current Athletic Code of Conduct (created 2004, revised 2015) is being replaced by a 2025 Athletic Handbook for Students aligned with the MHSAA handbook, incorporating coach/player/parent expectations, a CAP PACT (Coach-Athlete-Parent) agreement, and FinalForms, to be shared with the Board in spring. The department is also launching new ADA-compliant athletic websites for the district, Athens, and Troy High, and observes blackout dates for major holidays and religious/cultural observances, with no Sunday practices before 2:00 PM.
