https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared by Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent of Secondary Instruction, and Kristine Griffor, Assistant Superintendent of Elementary Instruction, this presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education (dated Tuesday, December 9, 2025) sets out recommendations for the district's Schools of Choice (SOC) program for the 2026-2027 school year. It notes that Schools of Choice provides non-resident students additional enrollment opportunities, that participation is optional for districts, and that the degree and extent of participation, including application/enrollment dates, grade levels, and building assignment, are determined locally.

Elementary enrollment projections were submitted by Plante Moran Cresa (Realpoint). The most-likely 2026-2027 projections shown include a kindergarten count of 766 (686 kindergarten / 80 preK) and a first grade of 739.

For 2025-2026, the district reported 173 elementary SOC students against 4,708 non-SOC students. By building, SOC counts were: Hill 39 (10.57%), Wass 25 (6.35%), Hamilton 22 (4.70%), Wattles 22 (5.54%), Costello 16 (4.04%), Troy Union 15 (3.90%), Leonard 13 (3.09%), Martell 11 (3.26%), Barnard 7 (1.73%), Morse 2 (0.51%), Bemis 1 (0.24%), and Schroeder 0. By grade, the 173 SOC students were: kindergarten 37, first 33, second 14, third 22, fourth 32, and fifth 35. SOC subgroup counts included 19 English Learners (10.98%), 94 Free/Reduced Lunch (54.34%), and 34 Special Education (19.65%); by ethnicity, SOC students were 96 White (55.49%), 28 Asian (16.18%), 22 Black (12.72%), 17 multi-ethnic (9.83%), 9 Hispanic (5.20%), and 1 Native American. Total non-SOC enrollment across grades K-12 was 11,165.

A survey emailed to current SOC families identified siblings age-eligible for kindergarten, first grade, and grades 6-8 in 2026-2027: for kindergarten, 8 under Section 105 (in-county) and 4 under Section 105c (out-of-county); for first grade, 0 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105c; and for middle school (grades 6-8 combined), 2 under Section 105 and 1 under Section 105c.

The recommendation is a Section 105 (in-county) proposal of 100 total slots, comprising 75 for kindergarten and 25 for first grade, plus 10 known siblings, and a Section 105c (out-of-county) proposal of 6 known siblings. Factors cited were current district enrollment, enrollment projections/patterns/trends, current SOC counts and percentages, projected age-eligible SOC siblings, and available elementary classrooms, along with a recommendation that the district use the Plante Moran Realpoint enrollment projection numbers.

What it is
The official 2026 Resolutions ballot from the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), provided to member districts including Troy for recording a board vote on proposed new and amended resolutions.

How resolutions are developed
- The OCSBA Government Relations Committee (GRC) establishes annual Legislative Priorities.
- The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee drafts new resolutions or amendments based on those priorities, referencing MASB and/or NSBA resolutions where aligned.
- After Board of Directors review, proposals go to member districts.

Voting rules
- Member districts vote only on new or amended resolutions; continuing resolutions are not re-voted.
- Each member district receives one vote.
- Resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member districts become the Association's official position.

Key dates
- Materials transmitted to members and Executive Assistants on November 18, 2025.
- Voting period open at least 40 calendar days.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Member District Ballot circulated by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) for its 2026 Resolutions, included in the Troy Board of Education's December 16, 2025 meeting materials so the board can record its vote.

Background and process: Annually, the OCSBA Government Relations Committee (GRC) establishes Legislative Priorities for the current legislative session. The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee then reviews the adopted priorities and drafts new resolutions and/or amendments to previously adopted resolutions based on them. Where there is alignment with MASB and/or NSBA resolutions, that resolution information is referenced. After review by the Board of Directors, the proposed resolutions are presented to member districts for consideration.

Voting rules: Member districts vote only on proposed new or amended resolutions; continuing resolutions are not subject to re-vote. Each member district receives one vote. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the Association as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors.

Voting period and deadline: The proposed resolutions, legislative priorities, and ballot were transmitted to every member and all member district Executive Assistants on November 18, 2025. The voting period remains open for at least forty (40) calendar days. Completed ballots had to be received no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, January 9, 2026, or the district's vote could not be counted.

Ballot content: The ballot poses the question, Does the Board of Education approve the proposed new and/or amended resolutions as presented, with checkboxes for YES (the Board approves all proposed new resolutions as presented) or NO (the Board does not). Spaces are provided for the district name, the meeting date, and a certification that the record is a true and correct record of the board's vote. Per OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2, member district votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees, and must be received before the deadline.

Submission: The completed and signed ballot is emailed to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org, signed by either the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board of Education and Superintendent. Questions are directed to Stefanie Crane at scrane@clarkston.k12.mi.us.

Adoption threshold
Under OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member districts become the association's official position.

Proposed new resolution #1 - Non-partisan school board elections
- OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections.

- OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, early intervention for infants and toddlers birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or risk of delay.
- Ties to Part C of IDEA (birth through age 2) and Michigan's Mandatory Special Education law (birth through age 25).
- Funding figures: estimated annual cost $230M; state should appropriate at least $138M (60%); Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides $48M.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
OCSBA's Proposed Amendments for January 2026, a five-page document (extracted text truncated near the end) distributed to Oakland County School Boards Association member districts, including Troy, for consideration alongside the 2026 Resolutions ballot. It opens by citing OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 (Resolution Adoption): resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

Two proposed new resolutions are presented.

Proposed new resolution #1: OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The rationale states it is in response to HB 4588, then moving through the state House (a link to the Michigan legislature bill page is provided). It argues that partisan school board elections would: decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, since board members would have to succeed in two elections (a primary as well as the November election); align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

Proposed new resolution #2: OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, described as an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale explains that the Michigan Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires special education services for eligible children from birth through age 25, and that federal law also mandates early intervention. It distinguishes IDEA Part B (special education services, ages 3 through 21) from Part C (early intervention for infants and toddlers birth through age 2), noting Michigan calls Part C Early On; supports for ages 22 through 25 fall under MMSE. Local communities receive Early On funding through their local Intermediate School District (ISD), with each ISD jurisdiction guided by an interagency coordinating council and local memoranda of understanding among education, mental health, public health, and social services. On funding, the document states the estimated annual cost is $230M to provide high-quality early intervention services; the state should appropriate at least $138M (60% of the estimated annual cost); and Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides state funding of $48M. It notes that for 50 years the association has advocated for IDEA funding and that the congressional promise to fund 40% of special education costs applies to both Part B and Part C.

The document then lists continuing resolutions previously adopted by members, with adoption and amendment dates noted. Two are visible before the text truncates: Accountability and Transparency (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025), which supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, extending to local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and colleges and universities (referencing MASB Resolution A 6.65); and Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025), supporting inclusion of broadband in any federal or state infrastructure plan and additional funding for affordable, reliable broadband access and internet-capable devices and software.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A resolution presented for adoption on the Troy Board of Education's December 16, 2025 consent agenda (item 5.E.), authorizing the district's participation in a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2026-2027 school year under Sections 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996. Under Michigan law, a school district must pass such a resolution each school year it intends to participate. The district anticipates a limited number of available seats for kindergarten, first grade, and grades 6-8, with the middle-school seats at Baker and Smith Middle Schools.

Section 105 (MCL 388.1705) provides students the option to enroll in another school district within the same intermediate school district as their own. Pursuant to Section 105, Troy School District will accept Schools of Choice applications from students who attend a district within Oakland County for the following seats: eighty-three (83) kindergarten, twenty-five (25) first grade, and two (2) total in grades 6 through 8.

Section 105c (MCL 388.1705c) provides students the option to enroll in another district that is within a different intermediate school district but shares a boundary line with their own ISD. Pursuant to Section 105c, Troy School District will accept applications from students who attend a district outside Oakland County, provided that district's ISD is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries, for: four (4) kindergarten, one (1) first grade, and one (1) total in grades 6 through 8.

The recommended action is to adopt the resolution, which resolves that the Board of Education of the Troy School District, exercising the option permitted by Sections 105 and 105c, will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2026-2027 school year for the stated seat counts: 83 kindergarten, 25 first grade, and 2 total grade 6-8 nonresident students who attend a school district within Oakland County; and 4 kindergarten, 1 first grade, and 1 total grade 6-8 nonresident students who attend a school district outside Oakland County whose intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries. The document provides blank Moved by and Supported by lines and Yes/No vote fields to be completed at the meeting.

Projects and buildings: Barnard Elementary School reroof of Roof Areas C & D; Leonard Elementary School reroof of Roof Areas A & E; Morse Elementary School reroof of Roof Areas E & F; Wass Elementary School reroof of Roof Area C; and a Restoration Package covering Baker Middle School, Bemis Elementary School, Hamilton Elementary School, Larson Middle School, Smith Middle School, and the Transportation Building.

The ten contractors are Christian Detroit, Division 7 Building Contractors, Great Lakes Roofing, JD Candler Roofing Company, MTD Construction, Newton Crane Roofing Inc, Royal Roofing, Royal West Roofing and Sheet Metal, Schena Roofing & Sheet Metal, and Sterling Roofing LLC.

Base bid amounts by project (lowest submitted amount noted first):
- Barnard (C & D): low of $207,000 (MTD Construction); other bids included $220,800 (Sterling), $252,449 (Great Lakes), $252,700 (JD Candler), $256,600 (Royal West), $286,600 (Schena), $291,062 (Division 7), $293,700 (Royal), $338,300 (Newton Crane), up to $475,000 (Christian Detroit).
- Leonard (A & E): low of $147,200 (Sterling); ranging up to $319,000 (Christian Detroit); Schena entered No Bid.
- Morse (E & F): low of $345,600 (Sterling); ranging up to $688,000 (Christian Detroit); Division 7 and Schena entered No Bid, and MTD withdrew its bid on 11/14/25.
- Wass (C): low of $88,000 (Sterling); ranging up to $215,000 (Christian Detroit).
- Restoration Package: low of $33,315 (Schena); other bids included $61,000 (Newton Crane), $63,000 (JD Candler), $64,453 (Great Lakes), $72,000 (Sterling), $109,800 (Royal), $132,000 (Christian Detroit), and $300,000 (MTD); Division 7 and Royal West entered No Bid.

The Bid Summary sheet records Total Low Bid Options: $895,076, attributed on the sheet to a combination of MTD, Great Lakes Systems, Royal West & Schena.

The Allowances sheet lists per-area allowances stated on the bid form alongside saddles missed in drawings: Barnard (Roof Area C $7,000 / $2,800; Roof Area D $4,000 / $4,200), Leonard (Roof Area A $5,000 / $0; Roof Area E $2,000 / $1,000), Morse (Roof Area E $7,500 / $9,500; Roof Area F $2,000 / $3,250), and Wass (Roof Area C $3,000 / $2,000).

The Unit Pricing sheet enumerates per-item unit rates by contractor for contingency work, including hourly labor rate (roughly $76.60 to $130), roof walkway pads, replacement roof drain bowls, clamping rings and strainers, wood nailer replacement by lumber size (2x4 through 2x10), interior protection, painting and repairing or replacing steel deck (22-gauge Type A and Type B), drain inserts, gypsum deck replacement, tapered and polyisocyanurate insulation, new roof drains and drain lines, and cementitious wood fiber (CWF) panel replacement. Several contractors listed certain items as T&M (time and materials) or Cost + 15%.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A presentation delivered at the December 9, 2025 Board Workshop on adopting new AP Spanish and AP French instructional resources through Vista Higher Learning. It notes the district's current AP texts - Abriendo Paso (2014) for Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for French - are outdated, lacking current cultural content, interpersonal speaking practice, and AP test prep. Guided by Oakland Schools consultant Jen Howe and a structured 2024-25 selection process, teachers evaluated Wayside, Klett, and Vista Higher Learning, recommending Vista because it matches AP-exam rigor, offers culturally relevant materials, holds about 80% of the AP World Languages market, and its authors are College Board trainers.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- Board Workshop presentation (12/9/25) on the AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption.

Context and rationale
- World Language sequence runs Levels 1-5, with Level 5 being AP; AP exams are written at the intermediate-high/advanced levels.
- AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate-level college course, assessing both language and culture across themes such as families and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges.
- Resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture; World Languages runs a 7-year adoption cycle.

Current resources (outdated)
- Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish - outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice, no AP test prep.
- T'es Branche (2014) for AP French - a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources.

Selection process
- Guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant.
- Timeline across 2024-25: exploration, leadership planning (8/11), department kickoff and visioning (8/20), rubric creation and vendor presentations (10/2, 10/7), pilot planning (10/20), PLC planning and check-ins (11/11, 11/18), and pilot feedback and synthesis (12/2).

Vendors considered
- Wayside - relatable, authentic content but does not match AP rigor; textbook only, no assessment practice.
- Klett - no AP resource for French; Spanish has authentic resources and AP practice but less rigor, fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology.
- Vista Higher Learning (recommended) - matches AP-exam rigor, culturally relevant, large resource bank; authors are College Board trainers; ~80% AP World Languages market share; will provide an updated crosswalk and free updated resources for the revised 2026-27 AP exam.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Slide presentation prepared for the December 9, 2025 Board Workshop titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, presenting the rationale and process behind a proposed adoption of new Advanced Placement world language resources.

Context and rationale: The district's world language sequence runs Levels 1 through 5, with Level 5 being AP; the AP exams are written at the intermediate-high/advanced levels. The presentation restates the TSD World Languages vision, describing learners who can communicate in an expanding global community, discover another culture's heritage, become resilient risk-takers, improve memory and problem-solving, strengthen college applications and professional marketability, and open opportunities for world travel. AP World Language and Culture is described as equivalent to an intermediate-level college course, cultivating understanding through interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational modes across themes including families and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture.

Current state: World Languages follows a 7-year adoption cycle, and with the PLC structure, Troy AP world language teachers want a common resource to build cohesion. Current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish - with outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice, and no AP test prep - and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, which is a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers have been pulling materials from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

Process of resource selection: The process was guided by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant, along an AP resources timeline spanning the 2024-25 school year: exploration of resources; leadership planning (8/11); department kickoff and visioning (8/20); rubric creation and vendor presentations (10/2 and 10/7); pilot planning (10/20); PLC planning and check-ins (11/11 and 11/18); and pilot feedback and synthesis (12/2).

Vendors considered, with pros and cons: Wayside offers relatable content with authentic resources for both French and Spanish but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is a textbook without assessment practice. Klett has no AP resource for French; its Spanish resource has many authentic resources and AP practice but does not match AP rigor, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology. Vista Higher Learning, recommended for both French and Spanish, matches the rigor of the AP exam, provides meaningful and culturally relevant resources plus a large resource bank (though resources may need scaffolding early in the year); its authors are also College Board trainers; it holds about 80% of the AP World Languages market share; and because the 2026-27 AP exam will be updated, Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk and, when it updates its textbooks, updated electronic and physical resources free of cost, with professional learning credit banked to support the change in August. The presentation closes with features of the recommended texts, including AP French culturally relevant resources and an AP Spanish cultural comparison exercise in which students compare the country studied with the United States.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's FY2025–26 General Fund Budget Amendment #1, presented January 13, 2026 by CFO Dan Trudel, CPA. It raises budgeted revenues to $197.9M and expenditures to $203.8M — a planned $6.0M deficit that draws the ending fund balance down to $27.7M (13.59%). The revisions are driven largely by state retirement (MPSERS) funding shifts, including the last-minute elimination of the $1.0M 147a(1) categorical and the loss of $5.1M in one-time 147a(4) pension-offset money.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Purpose
First budget amendment of FY2025–26, updating the General Fund and the district's other funds to reflect final state-aid, federal grant, and ISD allocations plus anticipated year-end expenditures.

Enrollment & foundation
Enrollment is 12,069.81 FTE, down 4.19 from the original budget. Foundation revenue rises $558,308 to $130,788,472.

MPSERS / state retirement
FY2025 included $5,055,278 of one-time 147a(4) pension-offset money that is eliminated in FY2026. For FY2026 the state removed the $1,007,246 147a(1) categorical at the last minute; employees no longer contribute the 3% healthcare premium (now absorbed by the district); pension UAAL costs fell 5.75% while the healthcare-subsidy expense rose 2.58% and normal cost rose up to 1.72%.

General Fund (Original → Amendment #1)
Revenues $190.5M → $197.9M; expenditures $194.3M → $203.8M; change in fund balance –$3.7M → –$6.0M; ending fund balance $29.2M → $27.7M (15.05% → 13.59%).

Other funds (amended change in fund balance)
Community Service –$0.55M; Preschool –$1.28M; Troy Career Center break-even; Food Service –$1.86M; Debt Fund +$0.20M. Prepared by Dan Trudel (dtrudel@troy.k12.mi.us).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Overview
This workshop presentation is the district's first General Fund Budget Amendment for fiscal year 2025–26, delivered by CFO Dan Trudel, CPA. Amendments true up the adopted budget to final revenue allocations and anticipated year-end spending. Four drivers are cited: categorical funding adjusted to the state aid status report; federal grant funding adjusted to final allocations; ISD-related funding adjusted to final allocations; and purchased services, salaries, and benefits adjusted to anticipated final expenditures.

Enrollment and foundation revenue
Blended enrollment is 12,069.81 FTE, a decrease of 4.19 from the original 12,074.00. The foundation allowance revenue increases by $558,308, from $130,230,164 to $130,788,472.

MPSERS and state retirement changes
The presentation devotes significant attention to Michigan Public School Employees' Retirement System (MPSERS) dynamics. In FY2025 the state provided $5,055,278 in 147a(4) funds to offset retirement expenses — a one-time categorical payment that does not roll into the future foundation allowance and is eliminated for FY2026. For FY2026, the state eliminated the 147a(1) categorical at the last minute, a $1,007,246 reduction; separately, employees no longer contribute the 3% healthcare premium, which the employer has absorbed this year, and anticipated state help to cover that 3% did not materialize. On the cost side, pension UAAL expenditures for districts were reduced 5.75%, the healthcare-premium subsidy expense increased 2.58%, and pension normal cost increased up to 1.72%.

General Fund bottom line
Budgeted revenues rise from $190,545,984 to $197,935,255, while expenditures rise from $194,285,613 to $203,763,818. The planned change in fund balance widens from –$3,739,629 to –$6,003,563. Beginning fund balance is $33,713,795 and the ending fund balance falls to $27,710,232, or 13.59% of expenditures (down from a projected 15.05%).

Other funds
The amendment also revises the Community Service Fund (ending balance ~$1.48M, change –$0.55M), the Preschool Fund (change –$1.28M), the Troy Career Center Fund (break-even), the Food Service Fund (ending balance ~$0.82M, change –$1.86M), and the Debt Fund (change +$0.20M, ending balance ~$4.17M). Contact: Dan Trudel, dtrudel@troy.k12.mi.us, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Rd., Troy, MI 48098.

This January 7, 2026 letter from Josh Eisenman, Project Manager at Barton Malow Builders (26500 American Dr., Southfield, MI 48034), to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services at the Troy School District (4420 Livernois Rd, Troy, MI 48098), recommends contract awards for BP#1D Elementary Bathroom Renovations (RFP 2526-12) and attaches the bid tabulation. On December 18, 2025, bid proposals were received and read publicly. Barton Malow reviewed the proposals with the project architect/engineer, TMP Architecture Inc. The project was advertised on the state website for about two and a half weeks, yielding a total of 40 bids. The scope includes all bathroom renovation work at Costello, Troy Union, Martell, and Schroeder Elementary Schools.

The recommended contractors and amounts are: 1A Demolition, Great Lakes Construction Services, $143,440; 1B Concrete, Culver Development, $48,000; 1C Painting, Seven Brothers Painting Inc, $43,650; 1D Flooring, Continental Interiors Inc, $93,315; 1E Hard Tile, Omega Floors, $149,500; 1F General Trades, Mid Thumb Contracting Group LLC, $312,424; 1G Mechanical, CSM Mechanical, $306,970; and 1H Electrical, Max Electric LLC, $178,000. The total contractor direct cost is $1,275,299, with an 8% contingency of $102,024, for a total construction cost of $1,377,323. Because Continental Contracting submitted an inaccurate bid and withdrew from the Painting category, Barton Malow recommends the second low bidder, Seven Brothers Painting Inc.

The attached tabulation lists competing bids. In Demolition, Great Lakes Construction Services ($143,440) was lowest, ahead of Global Green Services Group ($188,655), Mid Thumb Contracting Group ($235,973), Christman Constructors ($257,300), Blue Star ($282,750), and Reese Contracting ($290,000). In Concrete, Culver Development ($48,000) beat McCarthy Construction Company ($65,200) and DSP Constructors ($78,144). In Painting, Continental Contracting's withdrawn $37,502 bid was followed by Seven Brothers Painting ($43,650), Diamond Custom Painting ($45,090), GV Painting ($48,550), Twin Brothers Painting ($65,750), R&G Painting Home Improvements ($66,100), KV Painting ($84,275), and AGB Painting ($96,000). In Flooring, Continental Interiors ($93,315) led Shock Brothers Floorcovering ($96,350), Continental Contracting ($101,820), Omega Floors ($114,300), and Premier Tile Design ($115,250).
